schema_note: Queryable-tag discipline suggested by morpheus404 (Moltbook). kind=count|interpretation|assumption; tag=SOURCED|ASSUMPTION. Granularity: CELL-LEVEL since schema 1.1 - each count row carries exactly one figure (cell_of names the original composite row). Provenance: every row is inherited, not measured by the author - the cited source did the measuring; provenance_tier grades the source, witness_type states the author's relationship to it. Completeness: ASSUMPTION tags cover assumptions identified to date; this is NOT a complete inventory of the paper's assumptions. The ASSUMPTION fraction is a schema statistic about this ledger's bookkeeping, not a measure of evidential confidence in any claim. Interpretation and assumption rows are not measured cells; they carry alternatives_preserved. Current run: 30 rows, 24 count cells, 3 ASSUMPTION-tagged rows (I4, A1, A2).

rows.claim: Users choose federated/self-hosted options when NOT under shock
rows.value: OPEN: a tenure-defined subgroup of a self-selected 2023 survey retrospectively rates federation decisive for joining at 82-86%, robust to two cohort definitions, but timing attribution is unreliable (unresolved Musk anachronism, C19d) and portability preference is unmeasured by the instrument. This is NOT established non-shock-choice evidence. Revealed-preference non-shock choice of exit/portability itself remains unlocated. Exit may also be exercised without a failure event, so shock-timing is not a necessary frame - usage outside failure events could exist; none is located.

rows.notes: Research gate in paper ch08 8.9. Test: Bluesky non-shock cohort retention; Mastodon instance-level migration episodes with known non-shock causes.

rows.claim: Federation was a STATED pull among shock-era migrants (survey)
rows.value: 59.0% of respondents selected 'liking the idea of federated social media' as a reason they joined Mastodon; 70.3% among those who also selected 'looking for an alternative to Twitter'; 23.1% selected friends already on Mastodon
rows.denominator_definition: CU Boulder survey (Nicholson, Keegan, Fiesler et al.), N=1,343 after cleaning, self-selected via posts on Twitter/Mastodon/Bluesky
rows.notes: Exact answer-option wording preserved from the researchers' summary. 'Federated social media' as an answer option may bundle community, moderation, governance and portability - it does not isolate exit. The 23.1% friends figure alone does not establish network effects were not a pull (the survey's own analysis: network effects moor users to Twitter rather than pull to Mastodon). STATED preference, self-selected sample skewed toward users who felt strongly about Twitter changes (authors' caveat). Companion dataset: Cámara-Menoyo N=820 (doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/734YW), analyzed in C19.

rows.claim: Tenure-defined subgroup retrospectively rates federation decisive for joining
rows.value: 82% (146/177 answering) rated 'Mastodon is federated' Very or Somewhat decisive among respondents whose self-reported join tenure was >1 year before the survey
rows.denominator_definition: mastodon_age buckets 'More than three years ago' + 'Between one year and three years ago' (n=186) relative to field dates 2023-01-13 to 2023-04-13 (verified from repo readme), i.e. joining before ~early 2022, predating the Musk acquisition (announced 2022-04, closed 2022-10); instrument question: 'How decisive these factors were when you decided to join Mastodon?'
rows.notes: Author's computation from the public anonymized CSV (CC BY-SA 4.0, consent=Yes; NA = unanswered/not routed). RETROSPECTIVE STATED preferences of a tenure-defined subgroup; timing attribution unreliable (C19d). Joining before the Musk shock is not evidence of no other shock: no other incumbent shock for 2020-2021 identified under the author's search scope, which is not absence. 'Federated' may bundle community/moderation/governance/portability; this instrument offers NO portability/migration answer option, so portability preference is UNMEASURED here - federation preference is not portability preference.
rows.measurement_note: measured and reported by the cited source; inherited by the author (no direct observation of the underlying system)
